ASSIGNED FILES: /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1/kernel/sched/sched.c and /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1/kernel/locking/lock.c (ONLY these two files).
Task: Cooperative kernel core. Implement all stubs:
- sched.c: `void do_scheduler(void)` — cooperative round-robin: pick the next PCB from ready_queue, update current_running (per-CPU via get_current_cpu_id() if the code uses it), and switch_to context-switch; `void do_block(list_node_t *pcb_node, list_head *queue)` — dequeue pcb_node and enqueue it on the given block queue, mark the pcb TASK_BLOCKED; `void do_unblock(list_node_t *pcb_node)` — move the node back to ready_queue, mark TASK_READY.
- lock.c: `void do_mutex_lock_acquire(mutex_lock_t *lock)` — if the lock is held, block the current task on the lock's block queue and re-check after being woken (loop until acquired); set lock owner/status per the struct definition; `void do_mutex_lock_release(mutex_lock_t *lock)` — release the lock and wake waiter(s) per the existing design (check how many the tests/headers expect — look at the block queue handling).
Read include/os/sched.h, include/os/lock.h, the queue/list helpers (libs/ or kernel/sched/), and callers under kernel/syscall/ and test/test_project2/ to match the established API exactly.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1 && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles.

ASSIGNED FILES (all under /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2/): kernel/sched/sched.c, kernel/sched/time.c, kernel/locking/lock.c, kernel/locking/binsem.c, kernel/locking/futex.c (ONLY these files).
Task: Preemptive kernel core. Implement all stubs:
- sched.c: `void scheduler(void)` — preemptive priority-based scheduler: pick the highest-priority ready task (via max_priority_node), maintain ready_queue correctly, context-switch via switch_to; `list_node_t* max_priority_node(void)` — scan ready_queue and return the node of the task with the highest priority (check pcb_t priority field semantics in headers: whether lower or higher value wins, and any task->priority vs task->base_priority reset behavior the surrounding code implies).
- time.c: `void timer_check(void)` — walk the timer list, and for each expired timer (compare against get_ticks() or current time base used by the code) invoke its callback and remove/rearm per the struct design.
- lock.c: `void do_mutex_lock_acquire(mutex_lock_t *lock)` / `void do_mutex_lock_release(mutex_lock_t *lock)` — blocking mutex as in the cooperative design but integrated with this scheduler.
- binsem.c: `void binsem_op(int binsem_id, int op)` — BINSEM_OP_LOCK: block current task if the semaphore is taken; BINSEM_OP_UNLOCK: release and wake a waiter (constants in headers).
- futex.c: `futex_node_t* get_node(volatile uint64_t *val_addr, int create)` — hash val_addr into the bucket table, return matching node, allocate+init one if create and missing; `void futex_wait(volatile uint64_t *val_addr, uint64_t val)` — block current task on the node only if *val_addr == val; `void futex_wakeup(volatile uint64_t *val_addr, int num_wakeup)` — wake up to num_wakeup tasks blocked on that address.
Read include/os/*.h (sched, lock, futex, time), kernel/syscall/ callers, and test/test_project2/ to match exact semantics.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2 && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles.

ASSIGNED FILES: /workspace/Project1-Bootloader/createimage.c (the ONLY file you may modify).
Task: Bootloader image builder (host-side tool, compiled with host gcc, run as `./createimage --extended bootblock kernel`). Implement the two stubs: `static void write_segment(Elf64_Phdr phdr, FILE *fp, FILE *img, int *nbytes)` and `static void write_os_size(int nbytes, FILE *img)`.
Semantics: write_segment copies one loadable ELF segment from fp into img at the current image offset, padding up to a 512-byte boundary (sectors), and advances *nbytes by the padded byte count. write_os_size records the OS size in sectors at byte offset 508 of the image (the bootblock reads the sector count there) — see the reference implementation in /workspace/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1/tools/createimage.c (read-only reference, do NOT modify it): it rounds memsz up to 512, writes the segment bytes, and writes `nbytes/512 - 1` as a 2-byte value at offset 508.
Robustness requirement: the installed riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc emits extra non-PT_LOAD program headers (PHDR, INTERP, DYNAMIC, GNU_STACK, and zero-memsz ones) that make the naive reference implementation crash. Your implementation MUST: only write segments with p_type == PT_LOAD and p_memsz > 0, and copy via a fixed-size buffer loop (e.g. 512-byte chunks, zero-padding the final partial sector) rather than a variable-length array. Keep the printed output format consistent with the surrounding code.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project1-Bootloader && make CC=riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc must complete and produce ./image without crashing; then confirm with `xxd -s 508 -l 4 image` that a plausible non-zero sector count was written at offset 508, and that the image size is a multiple of 512.

ASSIGNED FILES (all under /workspace/Project3-Interactive_OS_and_Process_Management/): kernel/sched/sched.c, kernel/locking/binsem.c, kernel/syscall/mailbox.c (ONLY these files).
Task: Process management & IPC on the dual-core preemptive kernel. Implement all stubs:
- sched.c (6 stubs): scheduler with CPU-affinity masks (each pcb has a core mask; only schedule a task on a core its mask allows), plus process lifecycle: `pid_t do_spawn(task_info_t *task, void *arg, spawn_mode_t mode)` — allocate PCB+kernel/user stacks, init context and entry, enqueue ready; `void do_exit()` — mark current task exited, release its resources, wake its parent/waiters, reschedule; `int do_kill(pid_t pid)` — terminate the target process (handle blocked tasks, return success/failure per header contract); `int do_waitpid(pid_t pid, ...)` — block until the child exits then reap it (check the exact signature in the header/stub); and any other stub present (e.g. max_priority_node or affinity helpers).
- binsem.c: `void binsem_op(int binsem_id, int op)` — lock/unlock with per-process tracking of held semaphores (so do_exit can release them).
- mailbox.c: `int do_mbox_open(char *name)` — find or create a named mailbox, return id; `int do_mbox_send(int mailbox_id, void *msg, int msg_length)` — blocking send into a bounded circular buffer (block while full); `int do_mbox_recv(int mailbox_id, void *msg, int msg_length)` — blocking receive (block while empty); wake the opposite side after each operation.
Read include/os/sched.h, include/os/mailbox.h (or equivalent), the syscall table (kernel/syscall/syscall.c), and test programs under test/ to match exact semantics and constants (MAX_MAILBOX etc.).
Verify: cd /workspace/Project3-Interactive_OS_and_Process_Management && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles.

ASSIGNED FILES (all under /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/): kernel/mm/mm.c and kernel/sched/sched.c (ONLY these files).
Task: SV39 virtual memory with demand paging, plus VM-integrated process management. Implement all stubs:
- mm.c (8 stubs): `PTE* init_page_table(void)` — allocate and set up a fresh 3-level SV39 page table for a new process (map kernel space as the existing design requires); `ptr_t alloc_user_page(uint8_t pin, PTE *pgtable)` — allocate a physical user page (from the free-page pool; trigger NRU replacement/swap when exhausted); `ptr_t selete_page(void)` — NRU (not-recently-used) clock-style victim selection over the page frames, clearing accessed bits per the bookkeeping arrays present; `void write_to_sd(ptr_t pa)` — evict page at physical address pa to the swap area on the SD card (update swap bookkeeping); `void handle_page_fault(regs_context_t *regs, uint64_t stval, uint64_t cause)` — demand paging: allocate (or swap back in) the page for faulting va stval, map it, return to retry; `uintptr_t shm_page_get(int key)` — map/create the shared memory page for key into current process; `void shm_page_dt(uintptr_t addr)` — unmap it; `void free_process_user_page(PTE *pgdir)` — recursively walk and free all user pages of a process; plus any other stub.
- sched.c (6 stubs): `pid_t do_exec(const char *file_name, int argc, char *argv[], spawn_mode_t mode)` — find the task binary (embedded task info or image), create address space via init_page_table, load ELF segments, set up user stack with argc/argv, enter; `void do_exit()` / `int do_kill(pid_t)` / `int do_waitpid(...)` with page-table and swap resource cleanup; scheduler integration; any other stub.
Read include/os/mm.h, arch/riscv/include/asm/ (PTE bits, satp, sfence.vma helpers), the swap/page bookkeeping already present in mm.c, and the syscall table.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles.

ASSIGNED FILES: /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/drivers/net.c (the ONLY file you may modify). Another agent owns kernel/mm and kernel/sched in this project — do not touch them.
Task: GigabitEthernet network driver layer. Implement all stubs:
- `void do_net_send(uintptr_t addr, size_t length)` — transmit one packet: hand the buffer to the NIC (via the e1000/mac low-level helpers present in drivers/), handle DMA/descriptor bookkeeping, free/recycle the send buffer as the design requires.
- `long do_net_recv(uintptr_t addr, size_t length, int num_packet, size_t *frLength)` — receive up to num_packet packets into addr (each up to length bytes), recording each packet's length into frLength[]; support the blocking/poll semantics the surrounding code establishes (check the net receive queue/list and the wait logic), return the number of packets received (check header contract for the exact return convention).
- `void do_net_irq_mode(int mode)` — switch between poll mode and interrupt-driven mode (enable/disable the NIC interrupt and the PLIC/IRQ routing per the helpers in the codebase; in IRQ mode received packets are queued and blocked receivers woken — check how irq.c interacts with net.c).
Read include/os/net.h, drivers/mac.c/e1000.c (whatever low-level NIC code exists), kernel/irq/irq.c, and the syscall table + test/test_project5/ programs to match semantics exactly.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles (other agents' files may temporarily be stubs — stubs still compile, so a full build should succeed; if not, at minimum verify net.c itself compiles with the project's CFLAGS).

ASSIGNED FILES (all under /workspace/Project6-File_System/): kernel/fs/disk.c, kernel/fs/file.c, kernel/fs/fs.c (ONLY these files). Another agent owns kernel/mm and kernel/sched — do not touch them.
Task: Complete on-disk file system over the SD card. Implement all stubs:
- disk.c (4 stubs): `int mkfs(int print)` — initialize superblock, inode/block bitmaps, root directory on disk (and cache in memory per the existing globals); `uint16_t alloc_inode()` — find/clear a free bit in the inode bitmap, return inode id; `uint32_t alloc_block()` — same for data blocks; `void free_inode(uint16_t inode_id)` / `void free_block(uint32_t block_id)` — set bits back and sync the bitmap to disk per the design (check how the code flushes metadata: via bios_sd_write/kwrite wrappers present).
- fs.c (6 stubs): `int do_mkdir(char *dirname)`, `int do_rmdir(char *dirname)` (must be empty), `int do_ls(char *dirname, int mode, int *print_location_y)` (list entries; mode selects long format incl. inode details — check headers/tests for modes; print via the established output helper and advance *print_location_y), `int do_cd(char *dirname)` (update cwd inode; support ., .., absolute/relative per the path-parsing helpers present), `int do_link(char *filename, char *newfile, int mode)` (mode selects hard link = new dentry sharing inode with link count++, vs soft/symbolic link = new inode whose data holds the target path).
- file.c (5 stubs): `int do_touch(char *filename)` — create empty file dentry+inode in cwd; `int do_cat(char *filename, char *buffer)` — read whole file into buffer; `int do_fopen(char *filename, int access)` — allocate a file-descriptor slot (per-process fd table — check pcb_t), mode per access flags (read/write/append constants in headers); `int do_fread(int fd, char *buffer, int size)` / `int do_fwrite(int fd, char *buffer, int size)` — block-level I/O through the inode's direct (and indirect, if the struct has them) block pointers, honoring the fd offset and updating file size; handle partial blocks via a bounce buffer as the surrounding code implies.
Read include/os/fs.h (or include/fs*.h) for the on-disk layout (superblock_t, inode_t, dentry_t, sizes/offsets), the existing helper functions already present in these files (path lookup, dentry add/remove, block read/write wrappers), the syscall table, and test/test_project6/ programs to match semantics and return-value conventions exactly.
Verify: cd /workspace/Project6-File_System && make CROSS_PREFIX=riscv64-linux-gnu- main compiles.

lastPrompt: This is an operating-systems course lab (Projects 1–6) that implements a RISC-V bare-metal operating system. The repo spans six incremental projects: a bootloader, a simple cooperative kernel, a preemptive kernel with SMP, an interactive OS with process management and IPC, a virtual-memory-enabled kernel with demand paging, a device-driver layer with network support, and a file system. Entire subsystems have been removed and must be re-implemented. Your working directory is `/workspace`. The project code is already present in seven subdirectories: `Project1-Bootloader`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2`, `[redacted]`, `Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management`, `Project5-Device_Driver`, and `Project6-File_System`. Implement the following modules: The following modules need to be implemented or substantially built out. All stubbed function bodies contain `/* TODO: implement */`. Bootloader Image Builder (`Project1-Bootloader/createimage.c`): The host-side tool that reads ELF binaries and writes a bootable disk image. Two functions handle segment writing and OS size recording. (~1 file, 2 functions to implement) Part 1 Scheduler & Locking (`[redacted].c`, `kernel/locking/lock.c`): The cooperative round-robin scheduler, task blocking/unblocking primitives, and mutex lock acquire/release. (~2 files, 5 functions to implement) Part 2 Scheduler & Synchronisation (`Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2/kernel/`): The preemptive priority-based scheduler with ready-queue management, priority-based task selection, timer expiration checking, mutex locking, binary semaphore operations, and futex wait/wakeup with hash-based node management. (~5 files, 9 functions to implement) Process Management & IPC (`[redacted]/`): Multi-core scheduler with process lifecycle management (spawn, exit, kill, waitpid), priority-based scheduling with CPU affinity masks, binary semaphore tracking, and a mailbox-based inter-process communication system for sending and receiving messages with blocking semantics. (~4 files, 12 functions to implement) Virtual Memory Management (`[redacted].c`, `kernel/sched/sched.c`): SV39 three-level page table initialisation and teardown, user page allocation with NRU page replacement, swap-to-disk eviction, demand-paging page fault handling, shared memory mapping/unmapping, process creation/execution with ELF loading, and process termination with resource cleanup. (~2 files, 13 functions to implement) Device Driver Layer (`Project5-Device_Driver/drivers/net.c`, `kernel/mm/mm.c`, `kernel/sched/sched.c`): Network packet send/receive with poll and interrupt modes, IRQ mode switching, plus the full virtual memory and scheduler subsystems carried forward from Project 4 with additional page-helper functionality. (~3 files, 18 functions to implement) File System (`Project6-File_System/kernel/fs/`): A complete on-disk file system with superblock/bitmap-based allocation, inode and block management (alloc, free), directory operations (mkdir, rmdir, ls, cd), hard/soft linking, file operations (touch, cat, fopen, fread, fwrite), plus the full scheduler and virtual memory subsystems from Project 5. (~6 files, 24 functions to implement) The tests also depend on these signatures and entry points: The following functions are called or inspected directly by the test suite.
